# Executive Summary and Deliverables {#sec-executive-summary}

## Purpose of This Document

This document is the formal knowledge transfer package for the competitor bidding-behavior prediction system — comprising the **Competitor Intelligence** agent (the ML/rule-based prediction model and report generator) and the **Plan Reader** agent (the PDF-upload extraction and human-verification tool, see @sec-solution-architecture) — developed during the Carlson Analytics Lab's Summer 2026 engagement (delivered September 21, 2026) by Wenyu Zhong, Hsin Kuei Chang, Tobias Knight, and Jay Pederson for Central Specialties, Inc. (CSI).

Its purpose is to enable CSI to independently run, interpret, and maintain the prediction system **after the engagement ends**, with no ongoing consulting support beyond a 1–2 week transition window. This is a **handoff manual**, not a project retrospective: CSI will operate this on its own infrastructure and its own cloud API key, so every section should be written assuming the reader has no access to the team that built it.

::: {.callout-note}
**How to read this document.** For a business overview, read Chapters 1, 9, and 12. For technical implementation, read Chapters 3–7 and the Appendices. For running the report generator, go directly to Chapter 8. For ongoing maintenance, config changes, and troubleshooting, see Chapter 10.
:::

# Project Scope and Problem Definition {#sec-project-scope}

## Project Scope

This system gives CSI a way to see, ahead of a bid, who is statistically likely to compete for a given Minnesota-DOT-style highway letting, and how confident that read is — built from CSI's own historical bidding record rather than guesswork or a purchased industry list. It is one input to a bid/no-bid conversation, not a replacement for it: an estimator still makes the call, this system just gives them a data-backed second opinion to weigh against their own read of the market.

The scope of this work includes:

- ingesting a plan set (PDF) and extracting structured project facts, via the Plan Reader agent (@sec-solution-architecture);
- supporting a human verification/correction step over that extraction before a report is finalized;
- ingesting historical bid/project/competitor data;
- predicting competitor bidding probability for new projects via a supervised ML model;
- benchmarking that model against hand-written, first-principles rule-based models (distance, capacity, historical win-rate);
- generating LLM-based narrative reports explaining predicted competitors;
- supporting a parallel manual-entry path for client-specified top-3 competitors;
- providing update utilities for competitor records, pit/PID locations, and bid results; and
- documenting configuration, limitations, and maintenance guidance for independent operation.

This project does not connect to any live/automated bidding or letting system, does not automatically ingest new bid results (bid-result entry is a deliberate manual step — see @sec-limitations for why), and does not guarantee any specific Winner Hit Rate — see @sec-key-findings for what has and has not been validated against CSI's own stated expectations.

## Business Question

**Can CSI predict, ahead of a bid, which competitors are most likely to bid on a given project — and how does that compare to CSI's own manual competitor intuition?**

# Data Overview and Relationship Structure {#sec-data-overview}

## Data Sources

Row counts below are current as of this document's writing (`data/processed/`); they will grow as CSI enters new bid results, pits, and competitors through the update utilities in @sec-maintenance.

| File | Unit of Observation | Rows (current) | Role in Pipeline |
|:---|:---|---:|:---|
| `projects.csv` | One project/bid | 1,591 | Project metadata: location, type, material quantities, bid date |
| `bidder_results.csv` | One bid | 6,848 | Actual bidder, bid amount, win/loss outcome per project |
| Competitor name/entity registry (`competitor_name_registry - name_variants.csv`) | One raw name variant (898 rows → 715 canonical companies) | 898 | Canonical company identity, name variants, merge history |
| `MN_pit_list_cleaned.csv` | One material pit / PID | 2,398 | Pit location and ownership, used by the distance-based rule |

: Input data files used in the pipeline. {#tbl-input-files}

No additional client-provided reference files are consulted by the live pipeline beyond the four above — an earlier `reference/` folder of two supplementary competitor CSVs was evaluated and removed as dead weight (contributed zero unique data beyond what `bidder_results.csv` already covers) rather than kept as a fifth input.

## Historical Bid Data vs. Model-Predicted vs. Client-Entered Competitors

Three distinct "who might bid" concepts appear in this system and should not be conflated:

- **Historical bid data** — who actually bid, from `bidder_results.csv`. This is the ground truth used to train and evaluate everything else.
- **Model-predicted competitors** — output of the ML model and rule-based benchmarks, ranked by predicted bidding probability / rule score.
- **Client-entered competitors** — CSI's own top-3 picks via the user-input path, enriched with historical data but not produced by the model.

## Key Data Relationships

| Relationship | Join Key | Purpose |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `projects` → `bidder_results` | `project_natural_key` | Attach actual bidders/outcome to a project |
| `bidder_results` → competitor registry | `competitor_unit_id` | Resolve raw bidder name to canonical company identity |
| `projects` → pit/PID reference | project state + location | Support the distance-based rule |

: Key relational joins used in the pipeline. {#tbl-key-joins}

## Competitor Identity Resolution

Raw bidder names are standardized to a canonical `competitor_unit_id` via a name registry (fuzzy-matching + manual review), so the same company isn't double-counted under name variants (e.g., abbreviations, punctuation, mergers). This resolution step is the foundation for the competitor-list update utility described in @sec-maintenance — **any new competitor, merger, or renamed company must go through this same resolution step**, or it will silently create a duplicate entity rather than updating the existing one.

# Data Preparation and Key Data Issues {#sec-data-preparation}

## Preprocessing Workflow

Raw bid/project data is first passed through entity resolution (@sec-data-overview, Competitor Identity Resolution) so every bidder name maps to one canonical company. Candidate-pool construction then runs per-project, as-of that project's own bid date — no feature is ever computed using information that would not have been available before that date, so the train/validation/test split (`TRAIN_END_DATE = 2025-01-01`, `VALIDATION_END_DATE = 2025-05-01`) is a genuine time split, not a random one. The filtered candidate pool (used by the production ML model) is built from a 6-signal, weighted-fallback rule (`pipelines/ci_model/01_candidates/candidate_filter.py`): same-county history, same-project-type history, a 90-day recent-activity window, a 365-day historical-winner window, a 730-day fallback lookback for recurring regional bidders, and CSI's own priority-competitor flag — a competitor clears the pool if any signal fires strongly enough, or if their combined weighted score passes a threshold, so a company doesn't need to match on every signal to be considered.

## Candidate Pool Construction

Two different candidate-pool strategies exist in this system and are used for different purposes:

- **Filtered candidate pool** — historical rule-based pre-filtering (same-county/type/state history + recency) narrows the full competitor universe down before ranking. Used by the production ML model and rule heuristic.
- **Full-universe ranking** — no pre-filtering; ranks directly across the entire known competitor set (715 canonical companies as of this document's writing). Used specifically to test whether a single simple rule can reproduce CSI's stated intuition ("3–5 known competitors, winner is one of them ~90% of the time") without any filtering step. See @sec-methodology and @sec-key-findings.

::: {.callout-note}
These two strategies are not interchangeable, and Winner Hit Rate numbers are **not directly comparable** across them unless the candidate pool size is stated alongside the metric. See @sec-key-findings for the realistic-expectations discussion.
:::

## Key Data Issues

| Issue | Why It Matters | How We Handled It |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Competitor name variants / mergers | Same company can appear under multiple raw names over time, or two companies can merge into one going forward | Canonical registry + fuzzy-match confirmation workflow (see @sec-maintenance) |
| Pit/PID location data coverage is incomplete | Not every competitor has an owned pit on record, and location data may be geographically limited | Distance-based rule explicitly flags/degrades gracefully for competitors with no location on record — see @sec-methodology |
| No automated bid-result feed | Bid outcomes are not available via a reliable automated source | Manual bid-result input utility, by design — see @sec-limitations for rationale |
| The separate, file-based CLI report generator (@sec-report-guide) is only partly bridged to Plan Reader | It matches a project by a `--project-key` typed by hand against mostly-local files, not by a freshly verified plan's own database row | Its Capacity bullet pulls live from the same shared database Plan Reader writes to; the rest of it still needs a project already present in the local files it reads — see @sec-limitations |

: Key data issues and handling decisions. {#tbl-data-issues}

# Solution Architecture {#sec-solution-architecture}

## Two-Agent Design

The system is designed around two separate agents: **Plan Reader** and **Competitor Intelligence**.

- **Plan Reader** — takes a raw project plan set (PDF) and turns it into structured, queryable project facts. It runs a fixed four-stage pipeline: (1) convert the PDF to text (`01_pipeline/s1_convert.py`, a pure file transform, no model call), (2) chunk and embed that text locally into a searchable index (`s2_indexer.py`, MiniLM via Chroma — no API call), (3) a whole-document LLM extraction pass for fields with a predictable location (`s3_extract.py` — project location, work type, material quantities, bid date, route/milepost), and (4) a retrieval-backed LLM extraction pass for fields that are not on a predictable page (`s4_extract_rag.py`, falls back to searching the index). For the six states this system covers (MN/ND/SD/NE/IA/MT), the extracted route/milepost is additionally converted to a latitude/longitude via calls to that state's DOT GIS service. Every extracted field carries a confidence level and a source page, surfaced to the estimator in a **human verification step** before anything downstream is finalized — the estimator confirms or corrects the extraction, and any correction takes precedence over the automated value from that point forward. Once verified, the plan's record is written into CSI's shared Postgres database (`scratch.bid_projects`, tagged `row_source='plan_reader'`) — a durable row, not a one-off in-memory result.
- **Competitor Intelligence** — the agent documented in the rest of this chapter: predicts likely competitors for a project (ML model + rule-based benchmarks), generates narrative reports, and supports the update utilities.

::: {.callout-note}
**These two agents are connected through a shared database, not disconnected tools.** For the live, in-browser report: Competitor Intelligence's scoring (`competitor_predict_live.py::predict_report()`) is handed this specific plan's own just-verified data directly, and pulls its comparison signals (candidate pool, historical win rate, capacity) from that same shared `scratch.bid_projects`/`scratch.bid_results` database Plan Reader just wrote into — one connected pipeline through the database, not two isolated tools. The one real exception: the **separate, file-based CLI report generator** documented in @sec-report-guide (the tool that produces a standalone `.md`/`.docx` file) still runs mostly off local files and a `--project-key` typed by hand — only its Capacity bullet is pulled live from that same shared database. It cannot yet generate a file-based report keyed to a project that exists only as a Plan-Reader-written database row; see @sec-limitations, "The File-Based Report Generator Is Only Partially Bridged to Plan Reader."
:::

                                                                         │

## Model-Output Path: ML Model + Rule-Based Benchmarks

The production model is the 4-feature logistic regression documented in full in @sec-methodology
(county / type / state / size-fit). The rule-based benchmarks (distance-based, capacity-based,
historical win-rate-based) run alongside it as first-principles comparison points, also detailed in
@sec-methodology — see that chapter for the full feature list, fitted weights, and the benchmark
comparison against alternative models (36-feature logistic, decision tree, XGBoost).

## User-Input Path: Client-Entered Top-3 Competitors

::: {.callout-important}
This is an **explicit architectural fork**, not a fallback mode of the model-output path. CSI's manually entered competitors are enriched using the same historical reference data (win rate, recency, project-type history) but are never scored, ranked, or validated against the ML model's own predictions. If CSI wants to compare "what I think" against "what the model thinks," that comparison must be done manually today — it is not automated. See @sec-limitations.
:::

## LLM Report Generator

The report generator (`pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/`) takes the model-output path's predictions
(bidding probability + per-feature log-odds contributions) — it does **not** currently take
user-input-path (client-entered top-3) output as an input; see the callout above on that being an
unreconciled, separate fork. It runs as a command-line tool, detailed step by step in
@sec-report-guide, using model provider Anthropic (`claude-sonnet-4-6`, hardcoded in
`agent/orchestrator.py`, not user-configurable without editing that file).

| Component | Role |
|:---|:---|
| Planner | Selects which competitors (up to the requested top-N) get a full write-up for this project. |
| Executor | Computes each selected competitor's bid probability and pulls its supporting stats/log-odds contributions (`tools/predict_and_explain.py`). |
| Reflector | Mandatory self-critique pass on every drafted narrative — checks threat-label/probability consistency, that every claim is grounded in an actual stat, and no ML jargon leaked through; revises up to twice, flags for human review if still failing (`agent/reflector.py`). Full detail in @sec-methodology, LLM Report Generator Methodology. |
| Reporter | Assembles the final file (Project Introduction, Competitor List, Deep Dives) — see @sec-output-files for exactly what's in it. |
| System / polish / reflection prompts | Three plain-English `.txt` files under `06_reporting/prompts/` — the only part of this component non-technical staff can safely edit themselves. See @sec-maintenance. |

: LLM report generator components. {#tbl-report-generator-components}

::: {.callout-note}
No custom UI was built for CSI to tweak report *generation itself* — it runs from a command line
(@sec-report-guide), not a web form. The three update-utility web pages are a separate thing: they
let CSI add/correct data the reports draw from, not change how a report is written. See
@sec-maintenance for exactly what can and can't be self-edited.
:::

## Update Utilities

| Utility | What It Does | Fuzzy-Match / Confirmation Step? |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Competitor list update | Add, update, or merge company records | Yes — new or ambiguous names require confirmation before being added as a new entity |
| Pit / PID location update | Add, edit, or remove material pit/PID locations and ownership; includes a "find nearest pits" lookup against a project or address | No confirmation step — location edits are direct entry, but required-field validation and an access-company picker restricted to the competitor registry (@sec-maintenance) prevent free-text ownership typos |

: Update utilities. {#tbl-update-utilities}

## Configuration File

All parameterizable values live outside the model/report-generator code, split across three plain-English prompt files and two Python configuration files — not one single file, see @sec-maintenance's Configuration Authority section for the exact split and why. This includes system prompts, model version, and rule/threshold values. There is no custom UI for editing configuration — see @sec-maintenance for the field-by-field editing guide.

## Why Rule-Based Benchmarks Alongside ML

The rule-based models are not a fallback for the ML model — they exist to answer a specific diagnostic question: **can a single, explainable, first-principles rule reproduce CSI's stated intuition about who the real competitors are, without relying on a black-box model?** This was an open question posed by the faculty advisor as a deliberate "reverse baseline" experiment, not a production requirement. See @sec-methodology and @sec-key-findings for what was found.

# Methodology and Rule Logic {#sec-methodology}

## Supervised ML Model

The production model is a **4-feature logistic regression**, referred to in the codebase as the
"simple-rule baseline" (`pipelines/ci_model/03_training/train_simple_rule_baseline.py`,
`03_training/outputs/simple_rule_baseline_weights.json`). Its 4 inputs:

| Feature | Definition | Weight |
|:---|:---|---:|
| `county` | log1p(this competitor's historical win count in this county) | 2.1018 |
| `type` | log1p(this competitor's historical win count for this project type) | 0.6061 |
| `state` | log1p(this competitor's historical win count in this state) | 0.5647 |
| `size_fit` | how closely this competitor's typical historical material scale (mix tons, grading yards, etc.) matches the current project's active quantities | 0.4857 |

Coefficients are **data-fit**, not hand-picked: a `sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression`
(`class_weight="balanced"`, `C=1.0`) is trained on the same time-based train/validation/test split
used for every other model considered (train ends 2025-01-01, validation ends 2025-05-01).

::: {.callout-note}
**On the Weight column above.** These are the actual fitted values currently in
`03_training/outputs/simple_rule_baseline_weights.json` (intercept: -0.3977; fit on 92,929 training
rows), copied at the time of writing — they will change whenever the model is next retrained, so
treat the *feature list* as the stable contract and re-check the JSON file directly for the current
numbers rather than assuming these stay accurate. Whether/when this model gets retrained at all is
itself an open, unresolved question (see @sec-limitations) — these weights could be current for a
long time or could already be stale by the time this document is read.

These are **not** the same as the `3.0 / 2.0 / 1.0 / 1.0` illustrative weights shown in
`train_simple_rule_baseline.py`'s module docstring — that set is a **fallback**, only used if a
future retrain's train split is too small or single-class to fit a regression
(`MIN_FIT_ROWS = 50`). The values above are the real, currently-fitted production weights.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Why this model, not a more complex one.** Three alternatives were built and benchmarked against
it on the identical pre-filtered candidate pool and time split, using Winner Hit Rate@10 (share of
test-split projects where the actual winning bidder lands in the top 10 ranked competitors):

| Model | Feature count | Winner Hit Rate@10 (test, 209 projects) |
|:---|---:|---:|
| **4-feature logistic (production)** | **4** | **57.4%** |
| 36-feature logistic regression | 36 (adds pit-distance, per-material scope-match, recency windows) | 62.7% |
| Shallow decision tree (max depth 5) | 36 | 62.7% |
| XGBoost | 36 | 67.9% |
| Random ranking baseline | — | 5.4% |

The 36-feature alternatives buy real gains over the 4-feature model: roughly **5 percentage points**
for the 36-feature logistic regression and the shallow decision tree (62.7% vs. 57.4%), and roughly
**10 percentage points** for XGBoost (67.9%). None of it was judged worth the loss of
interpretability: a 36-feature score mixes pit-distance and material-scope-match terms that are hard
for an estimator to sanity-check by eye, while the 4-feature score reduces to a plain, auditable
statement — "how often has this competitor won here / for this project type / in this state, and
does their typical job size match this project" — with coefficients an estimator can read directly
off the model file.

**The more complex alternatives (36-feature logistic, decision tree, XGBoost) were built and
evaluated but are intentionally not wired into the live report-generation pipeline.** They remain
in the repository purely as comparison/evaluation artifacts (`03_training/outputs/*.json`,
`04_evaluation/outputs/winner_hit_rate_metrics.csv`) so the choice of the simpler model stays
checkable, not because they were abandoned mid-build. A linear SVM was also evaluated in earlier
work but is excluded from this comparison — retraining it to match the current pool-matched split
was judged not worth the cost of one more comparison point; it remains in the repo
(`03_training/train_svm.py`) as a non-benchmarked artifact.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Methodology.** Every row in the table above is computed from a single evaluation run
(`04_evaluation/outputs/winner_hit_rate_metrics.csv`, produced by
`pipelines/ci_model/04_evaluation/evaluate_ranking.py`) against the identical 209-project
winner-in-pool test split — the subset of the current test-period projects where the actual
winning bidder is present somewhere in the candidate pool at all (`build_winner_hit_rate()`, which
drops any project where the winner never reached the pool). All four scored models share this same
denominator, so the table is directly comparable row to row.
:::

## Rule-Based Benchmark Models

Three first-principles, single-factor rules were built specifically to test whether one dominant signal could reproduce CSI's competitor intuition without any candidate pre-filtering (full-universe ranking, see @sec-data-preparation):

| Rule | Definition | Known Coverage Caveat |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Distance-based | Ranks competitors by distance from their nearest owned material pit to the project site | Pit-ownership location data currently covers a subset of competitors and a subset of geography — competitors without a recorded pit location cannot be ranked by this rule alone |
| Capacity-based | Ranks competitors by `log(1 + total historical bid dollar volume)` as of the project's bid date — raw historical scale, no project-fit involved | None specific to this rule; every competitor with any bid history gets a score |
| Historical win-rate-based | Candidate pool restricted to same-state history only (no cross-state selection); scored by win rate for the project's type within that state | Companies with no in-state bid history cannot be scored by this rule |

: Rule-based benchmark definitions. {#tbl-rule-definitions}

::: {.callout-note}
**Two capacity-based variants were actually tested, not one — this table reports the winner.**
`pipelines/ci_model/experiments/first_principles_rules/` built and evaluated TWO single-factor
capacity rules on the identical full-universe (no pre-filtering) pool, 243 projects:

| Variant | Definition | Winner Hit Rate@10 |
|:---|:---|---:|
| **`capacity_volume` (used above)** | `log(1 + total historical bid dollar volume)`, pure scale, no project-fit | **25.0%** |
| `capacity_size_fit` (rejected) | Company's historical average material quantity vs. this project's required quantity (log-gap fit score, only over materials the project actually needs, ≥3 prior bids/material required) | 1.3% |

`capacity_size_fit` was rejected on real evidence, not a coin flip: an early version scored *worse
than random* (winner's average rank percentile 0.63 vs. 0.5 random) due to a `NaN`-handling bug
that silently scored most of the ~700-company pool off missing-material columns; after fixing that
bug the rank percentile improved to 0.37 (better than random) but the Hit Rate@10 stayed at 1.3% —
matching a project's material scale to a company's historical average is a materially weaker
"who wins" signal than raw company scale. Full bug writeup and re-run script:
`pipelines/ci_model/experiments/first_principles_rules/README.md`.

**Confirm before delivery**: the Deliverables table (@tbl-deliverables) lists one "capacity-based"
rule, singular. `capacity_volume` is what this document assumes ships as that rule (it is the one
carried into the comparison table below and is the only variant the codebase's own README calls
"the strongest single factor") — but that is this document's inference from the evaluation results,
not a recorded team decision. Confirm this is in fact what CSI receives, or state explicitly if both
variants ship.

**On the ~90% question**: none of the four single-factor rules came remotely close to CSI's stated
~90% expectation on their own —

| Rule | Winner Hit Rate@5 | @10 | @20 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| `capacity_volume` | 17.9% | 25.0% | 29.9% |
| Distance-based | 14.7% | 15.2% | 15.2% |
| Historical win-rate-based | 1.4% | 1.8% | 3.2% |
| `capacity_size_fit` (rejected variant) | 0.0% | 1.3% | 5.8% |

All four sit well below the composite 4-feature production model (39.7%/57.4%/68.4% at @5/@10/@20,
§Supervised ML Model above) and the ML models. See @sec-key-findings for the full discussion of why
no single factor reproduces CSI's intuition. Source:
`pipelines/ci_model/experiments/first_principles_rules/outputs/summary.csv`.
:::

## LLM Report Generator Methodology

The narrative-writing step (`06_reporting/agent/`) is a small three-stage pipeline that turns the
model's numeric output into a plain-English paragraph per competitor — it never re-scores or
re-ranks anything; scoring is finished before this stage ever runs.

1. **Inputs — probability + feature importance, not raw model internals.** For each competitor,
   `tools/predict_and_explain.py` computes the bid probability and a per-feature **log-odds
   contribution** (`raw_contributions`), then splits those into `top_reasons_to_bid` /
   `top_reasons_not_to_bid` (sorted descending/ascending, zero-contribution features excluded). Only
   these — the probability, the threat level (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW) derived from it, and the named top
   reasons — are ever handed to the LLM. The model's coefficients, feature names in raw form, and any
   other internals never reach the prompt.
2. **Drafting — one fixed system prompt, one per-competitor user prompt.**
   `06_reporting/prompts/system_prompt.txt` sets hard rules the model must follow for every
   narrative: no ML/statistics jargon ("no 'logistic regression', 'coefficients', 'z-scores',
   'features', 'model output'"), ground every claim in the specific signals provided, don't add
   unlisted information, and treat probability as a plain likelihood band (>70% high, 40–70%
   moderate, <40% unlikely). `06_reporting/prompts/polish_prompt.txt` then feeds in the competitor
   name, bid likelihood, threat level, and a bullet-point rendering of the top signals
   (`tools/generate_narrative.py`), asking for 2–3 plain-language sentences referencing specific
   numbers from those signals only.
3. **Reflection/polish — a mandatory self-critique pass, not optional.**
   `06_reporting/agent/reflector.py::reflect()` runs a second LLM call
   (`prompts/reflection_prompt.txt`, `temperature=0.0`) against every drafted narrative, checking
   five things: threat-level/probability consistency (HIGH requires ≥70%, MEDIUM 40–69%, LOW <40%),
   every claim grounded in an actual signal value, no ML jargon, no logical contradictions, and every
   scope-match claim (paving/grading/structure/etc.) actually present in the signals list. A failed
   check returns a revised narrative, which is re-checked; up to `MAX_REVISIONS = 2` attempts. If
   still failing after 2 revisions, the narrative is flagged `reflection_passed: False` for human
   review rather than shipped silently — this failure mode has an explicit code path, not a bare
   assumption that the LLM got it right.

## Winner Hit Rate as the Benchmark Metric

Winner Hit Rate@K = the share of projects, among those with a resolvable winner, where the actual winning bidder appears in the top K predicted/ranked competitors. This is the primary metric used to compare the ML model, rule-based benchmarks, and (informally) CSI's own stated intuition.

::: {.callout-important}
Winner Hit Rate depends heavily on candidate pool size and definition. A rule evaluated on a small, pre-filtered pool and a rule evaluated on the full competitor universe are **not comparable** on this metric without stating the pool size. See @sec-key-findings for the full discussion of this as an open experimental question.
:::

\newpage

# Output Files and Interpretation Guide {#sec-output-files}

::: {.callout-note}
**How to read this chapter if you've never opened a code file before.** Everything below describes
a single result: one plain-text report about one project, sitting in one folder on the computer that
runs this system. You do not need any programming knowledge to open or read it — you need to know
which folder to look in and what the sections inside mean. That's what this chapter is for.
:::

## Output File Inventory

Every time the report generator runs (see @sec-report-guide), it produces **one file** — not a
dashboard, not a database, not something you check inside the web browser. That file lands in this
folder on disk:

```
pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/outputs/reports/
```

| Output File | One File Per | Created By | How to Open It |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `bid_report_<project key>.md` | One project | Running the report generator (default format) | Any plain-text editor (Notepad, TextEdit), or a free Markdown viewer. It is readable as-is even in a plain text editor — the `#`/`##`/`-` symbols are just section markers, similar to how you might use ALL CAPS or dashes in an email to organize it. |
| `bid_report_<project key>.docx` | One project | Running the report generator with the `--format docx` option | Microsoft Word — opens like any other Word document. |

: Output file inventory. {#tbl-output-files}

The "project key" in the filename is the same identifier used to run the report — see
@sec-report-guide. Each run creates a new file (or overwrites the old one with the same name);
nothing is deleted automatically, so old reports for the same project stay unless someone removes
them by hand.

::: {.callout-important}
**This is a separate thing from the live web app.** If your team also uses the chat-based web app
(where you drop in a PDF plan and chat with it), that produces its OWN report, shown directly in
your browser — it does not create or read these `.md`/`.docx` files, and this generator does not
touch what you see in the browser. The two are related in *purpose* (both analyze competitors for a
project) but are two separate tools with two separate outputs. Do not expect a file from one to show
up in the other.
:::

## Key Field Dictionary

Opening the file, you'll find it organized top to bottom like this (matching what a real generated
report actually contains — not a hypothetical schema):

| Section (as it appears in the file) | What's in it, in plain terms |
|:---|:---|
| **Bid Intelligence Report** (title) + project line | Project ID, county/state, the bid date, and when this report was generated. |
| **PROJECT INTRODUCTION** | The project's location, its "Work Type" (a plain-English category like *Mill & Overlay* or *Reconstruct / Rebuild* — see the small reference table right below it in the same file for what each type means), coordinates, and a note on nearby material pits (public-access and, separately, any private pits owned by a listed competitor). |
| **COMPETITOR LIST** | Two groups: **Priority Competitors** (companies CSI already tracks as known, frequent competitors) and **Discovery Competitors** (companies the system found in the historical data as plausible bidders, that aren't on CSI's known-priority list). Both groups are just names at this point — the detail is below. |
| **Deep Dives** (one block per competitor, under a `###` heading with the company name) | Five to six plain-language stats for that one company, always in this order: |
| — Bid Rate | How often this company bids at all, out of everything it *could* have bid on (e.g. "11% historically — highly selective"). |
| — Recency | Whether they've bid recently (e.g. "actively bidding — last bid within 30 days") or gone quiet. |
| — Capacity | Whether their typical workload this season looks lighter or heavier than usual, if there's enough history to say. |
| — Experience | How many times they've bid this *exact* type of project before. |
| — Win Rate (by project type) | Their win percentage on this project type, with the raw count (e.g. "26% — 14 wins from 53 Mill & Overlay bids"). |
| — Win Rate (by county) | Same, but narrowed to this specific county — often shows "insufficient data" if there have been fewer than 3 bids there, which is intentional (see below), not a bug. |
| — *(LLM-enhanced runs only, see @sec-report-guide)* Bid Likelihood, Threat Level, and a 2–3 sentence written explanation | A % likelihood this company bids, a HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW label, and a short plain-English paragraph explaining why — written by an AI model, always grounded in the stats immediately above it, never introducing a number that isn't already in this same file. |

: Key field dictionary. {#tbl-key-fields}

## Recommended Interpretation Rules

1. **"Insufficient data" is the system being honest, not broken.** When a stat says "fewer than 3
   bids — insufficient data," that's a deliberate floor: the system refuses to state a win rate off
   1 or 2 data points because that number would be meaningless (a company that bid once and won
   would otherwise show "100% win rate," which is misleading). Read this the same way you'd read a
   blank cell in an Excel pivot table with too few rows to summarize — it means "not enough history,"
   not "zero."
2. **A HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW threat label and its % likelihood always agree, by rule, not by chance.**
   HIGH always means ≥70% likelihood, MEDIUM 40–69%, LOW under 40% — a second AI pass specifically
   checks this consistency on every report before it's finalized (see @sec-report-guide's "Reflection
   Pass"). If you ever see a label that doesn't match its own percentage, treat that report as
   something to flag, not something to trust.
3. **Priority vs. Discovery is not a ranking of importance.** "Priority" means CSI already has this
   company flagged as a known competitor; "Discovery" means the system found supporting bid history
   for them but they aren't on that known list yet. A Discovery competitor can still have a higher
   bid likelihood than a Priority one — read the individual stats, not just which group a name is
   filed under.
4. **A written narrative sentence is an explanation of the numbers above it, not a separate opinion.**
   Per the system's own writing rules (@sec-report-guide), it is not allowed to introduce any claim
   that isn't already backed by one of the stats in that same deep-dive block. If a sentence seems to
   claim something the stats don't support, that's worth flagging for review — it should not happen
   by design, but "should not happen by design" is not the same guarantee as "cannot happen."
5. **This is one project's report, not a season-wide comparison.** The stats inside are all scoped
   to the one project named at the top. Comparing a "Win Rate" number from one project's report
   against a different project's report is comparing two different scopes (different work types,
   different counties) and will not mean what it looks like it means.

# Report Generator User Guide {#sec-report-guide}

::: {.callout-important}
**Read this before anything else in this chapter.** Unlike the three update tools in
@sec-maintenance (which are ordinary web pages — click a button, fill in a box, exactly like
updating a spreadsheet through a form), running the report generator today means typing an exact
line of text into a "Terminal" or "Command Prompt" window and pressing Enter — the same kind of
black window a software developer works in, not a web page. **This is not something we recommend a
first-time, non-technical user attempt alone.** If something is typed slightly wrong, the result is
a page of red technical error text (shown as-is below, not simplified), not a friendly "please check
this field" message the way Excel or a web form would show you.

**Our recommendation**: during the transition window, CSI should designate one person — whoever is
most comfortable following exact, copy-pasteable instructions on a computer (even someone with no
programming background can do this if they follow the steps below exactly and don't improvise) — as
the person who runs this tool. Steps below are written to be followed exactly, character for
character, by that person.
:::

## How to Run the Report Generator

**What you need before you start**: the exact "project key" for the project you want a report on —
a text ID that looks like `MN_STEARNS_CO_MELROSE_2023-08-03` (STATE _ COUNTY _ CITY _ DATE). There is
currently no search box for this — it has to be looked up by opening
`data/processed/projects.csv` (a spreadsheet-style file — it can be opened directly in Excel) and
finding the row for the project you want, then copying its `project_natural_key` column value
exactly.

**The exact command** (this whole block, typed or pasted as one line, from the very top folder of
the project — ask your technical contact/IT to confirm you're in the right folder first if unsure):

```bash
python pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/agent/orchestrator.py \
  --project-key MN_STEARNS_CO_MELROSE_2023-08-03 \
  --predictions "pipelines/ci_model/03_training/outputs/ranking_predictions.csv" \
  --model "pipelines/ci_model/03_training/outputs/simple_rule_baseline_weights.json" \
  --registry "pipelines/ci_model/01_candidates/outputs/competitor_name_registry - name_variants.csv"
```

Replace only the text after `--project-key` with your own project's key — do not change anything
else in the line, including the quotation marks.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Do not omit the `--predictions`/`--model`/`--registry` parts to "keep it simple."** The tool has a
built-in fallback that LOOKS like it should work without them, but that fallback points at a folder
that does not actually exist in this delivery — running the shorter version WILL fail with a
`FileNotFoundError`. Always include all four lines above.
:::

What happens next depends on one thing: whether an Anthropic API key is set up on this computer.

- **If it is set up**: the tool takes roughly a few minutes per report (it's contacting an AI
  service, one call per competitor, so more competitors = more time) and produces a report with
  full written explanations for each competitor.
- **If it is not set up** (or CSI has chosen to run without one): the tool automatically falls back
  to a faster, no-AI version — same facts and numbers, just without the written explanation
  sentences — and finishes in seconds. It tells you this is happening; you do not need to do
  anything differently.

**What success looks like** — you should see something like this scroll by in the window, ending
with a line telling you exactly where the file was saved:

```
============================================================
  CSI Bid Intelligence Agent
  Project: MN_STEARNS_CO_MELROSE_2023-08-03
============================================================
  Tier 1 (priority): 25  |  Tier 2 (discovery): 13
[1/4] Planner — selecting top 3 competitors...
[2/4] Executor — running predictions and narratives...
[3/4] Reflector — quality checking narratives...
[4/4] Reporter — assembling report...
============================================================
  Report saved: .../pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/outputs/reports/bid_report_<your project key>.md
============================================================
```

**What failure looks like**: a block of red/orange text ending in a line starting with an error type
(most commonly `FileNotFoundError` — one of the four lines above was typed wrong or a file has moved
— or `ValueError: No rows found for project_natural_key=...` — the project key was mistyped or
doesn't exist in the data). There is no friendly rewording of these messages today; if you see one,
double-check the project key against `projects.csv` first, and if it still fails, that's the point
to bring in technical support rather than keep guessing at the command.

## Report Sections

See @tbl-key-fields in @sec-output-files for the full field-by-field breakdown of what's inside the
finished file — Project Introduction, the Priority/Discovery competitor list, and a Deep Dive block
per competitor (bid rate, recency, capacity, experience, win rate, and — only when the AI-written
version ran — a likelihood percentage, a HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW label, and a short written explanation).

## Recommended Review Workflow

1. Confirm the project key matched the project you actually meant (check the county/date printed at
   the top of the finished report against what you expected).
2. Read the Priority Competitors first — these are the names CSI already watches closely.
3. For each HIGH-threat competitor (or, in the no-AI version, each competitor with a high recent bid
   rate and recent activity), sanity-check the stats against what your own team already knows about
   that company. The system is built to explain itself with real numbers specifically so this
   sanity-check is possible — if a claim doesn't match what you know, that's useful signal, not
   something to silently override.
4. Treat "insufficient data" entries as missing information, not as a "no" answer (see
   @sec-output-files, Recommended Interpretation Rules).

## Interpretation Warnings

- The written narrative sentences (when present) are generated by an AI model reading the numeric
  stats already in the same report — read them as a plain-language SUMMARY of those numbers, not as
  a separate, independently-researched opinion. Everything the narrative claims should already be
  traceable to a number sitting right above it in the same competitor's block.
- A second, automatic AI pass checks every narrative for consistency (does the HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW label
  actually match the stated likelihood percentage? does every claim trace back to a real number?)
  before the report is finalized — but this is a quality check, not a guarantee. If something reads
  as inconsistent or unsupported, flag it rather than assume the check must have caught it.
- This tool and the separate, browser-based plan-upload chat tool (if CSI also uses that) are two
  different systems that do not share outputs — see the callout in @sec-output-files.
- The report reflects the historical bid data files this tool reads (`data/processed/`,
  `pipelines/ci_model/*/outputs/`) as of whenever those files were last regenerated. **Entering a
  new bid result through the web update tool (@sec-maintenance) does NOT automatically flow into
  this report generator** — see the data-flow warning in @sec-maintenance before assuming a recent
  entry will show up here.

# Key Findings and Business Implications {#sec-key-findings}

## Finding 1: County-Level Win History Is the Strongest Single Signal in the Production Model

Of the production model's 4 features (@sec-methodology), `county` carries the largest fitted weight (2.1018) — roughly 3.5x the `type` weight (0.6061), 3.7x the `state` weight (0.5647), and 4.3x the `size_fit` weight (0.4857). In plain terms: a competitor's history of winning **in this specific county** is, by a wide margin, the single most predictive fact the model has about whether they'll bid again — well ahead of their track record on this project type generally, their statewide presence, or how closely the project's material scale matches their typical job size. This matches an intuition CSI estimators likely already hold informally (local players stay local), but it is useful to have it confirmed as the dominant quantitative signal rather than an assumption: it means data-entry accuracy on county is disproportionately important to this system's usefulness, more so than any other single field.

## Finding 2: The Distance-Based Rule's Real-World Usefulness Is Capped by Pit-Ownership Data Coverage

The distance-based rule (@sec-methodology) ranks competitors by proximity from their nearest owned material pit — but the pit-location reference data behind it (`MN_pit_list_cleaned.csv`) is 100% Minnesota: every one of its 2,398 rows is an MN pit, while the project dataset spans 6 states (IA, MN, MT, ND, NE, SD). The rule can only ever be meaningfully applied to Minnesota projects today. Even within Minnesota, ownership is recorded for a minority of pits: of the 2,398 rows, 1,524 (63.6%) have `unknown` access/ownership, 433 (18.1%) are `open`-access, and only 258 (10.8%) are tagged to a specific competitor. This is not a flaw in the rule's logic — it is a data-coverage gap, and it is the direct, measured reason the distance-based rule's own Winner Hit Rate underperforms the composite model (@sec-methodology, Rule-Based Benchmark Models). Expanding pit-ownership coverage, geographically and by known-owner percentage, is the single highest-leverage data investment for improving this specific rule — see @sec-future-recommendations.

## Finding 3: The Production Model Is the Simplest of Four Tested, Not the Most Accurate

Four candidate models were built and benchmarked on the same pre-filtered candidate pool and
train/validation/test split (see @sec-methodology for the full table): a 4-feature logistic
regression, a 36-feature logistic regression, a shallow decision tree, and XGBoost — all on top of
the same 36 underlying engineered features except the 4-feature model, which uses only historical
win counts by county/type/state plus a project-size-match term. (A linear SVM was also evaluated in
earlier work but is excluded from this pool-matched comparison — see @sec-methodology.)

The 4-feature model was selected for production despite scoring roughly 10 percentage points lower
on Winner Hit Rate@10 than the best-performing alternative, XGBoost (57.4% vs. 67.9% on the
209-project test split). This was a deliberate interpretability-over-accuracy trade-off, not an
oversight: the 4-feature model's score is a plain, human-checkable combination an estimator can
audit by eye, whereas the accuracy gain from the more complex models comes from pit-distance and
material-scope features that are harder to explain in a client-facing narrative report. The other
three models remain in the repository as evaluation artifacts (not wired into the live pipeline) so
this trade-off stays checkable rather than a one-time decision that can't be revisited.

::: {.callout-note}
**Approval status.** The pool-mismatch data-integrity issue previously flagged here has been
resolved — all four models in the table above (@sec-methodology) are now evaluated on the same
209-project pool-matched test split. These specific numbers still require the team's sign-off
before external/client-facing use.
:::

## Finding N: Winner Hit Rate Is an Open Experimental Question, Not a Confirmed Finding

::: {.callout-important}
**This finding is tentative.** It reflects a preliminary internal experiment, not a validated, sign-off-ready conclusion. The direction (no single rule matches CSI's ~90% intuition) held across what was tested so far, but the scope, dataset, and methodology have not been finalized — this should not be presented to CSI as settled without further validation and team review.
:::

CSI's stated intuition — that the true winner is one of 3–5 known competitors roughly 90% of the time — was treated as a hypothesis to test, not a target the system was guaranteed to hit.

What was tested (preliminary, internal):

- A composite rule-based score (combining county/type/state history + project-size fit) ranking directly over the full, unfiltered competitor universe.
- Individual first-principles rules in isolation: distance-only, capacity-only, and state-restricted historical win-rate-only.
- The production ML model and existing rule heuristic, evaluated on a pre-filtered candidate pool.

The specific per-rule Winner Hit Rate@5/@10/@20 numbers behind this finding are already tabulated in @sec-methodology (Rule-Based Benchmark Models, "On the ~90% question") — they are internal experiment results, not yet approved for external/client-facing use as final figures; do not reuse them outside the team without sign-off, since methodology and date ranges may still differ from the frozen delivery dataset.

The tentative, qualitative observation across this preliminary experimentation was that **no single factor in isolation reproduced anything close to CSI's stated ~90% expectation** — combining signals (geography + project-type history + recency, or a trained ML model) outperformed any individual rule tested so far. This should be communicated to CSI as an open, still-being-investigated question rather than a validated benchmark result, and revisited once the team confirms the methodology and dataset are final.

## Methodology Notes and Validation Items Before Operational Use

Open items the team should resolve, or CSI should ask about, before treating this system's outputs as settled:

- **Confirm the capacity-rule variant.** @sec-methodology documents two capacity-based rule variants tested (`capacity_volume`, used; `capacity_size_fit`, rejected). This document assumes `capacity_volume` is what ships — confirm that is in fact the intended production default.
- **Model-comparison table pool mismatch — resolved.** The 4-feature production model's Winner Hit Rate figure and the alternative models' figures (36-feature logistic, decision tree, XGBoost) are now all evaluated on the same 209-project pool-matched test split (@sec-methodology). Linear SVM was excluded rather than retrained to match, as not worth the cost of one more comparison point.
- **Confirm the frozen delivery dataset.** Several numbers in this document (row counts in @sec-data-overview, the Winner Hit Rate tables) reflect the dataset as of this document's writing. If additional bid results, projects, or competitors are loaded before final delivery, re-pull these numbers rather than assume they still hold.
- **Verify the CI-data admin features against a real production database.** As of this document's writing, the three update-utility web pages (@sec-maintenance) have passed all automated code checks but have not been exercised end-to-end against CSI's live database — see @sec-limitations.
- **Decide whether/when to enable the CY/SY quantity-conversion feature.** See @sec-limitations, "Some Extracted Bid-Item Quantities Are Withheld, Not Converted, by Design" — this is a deliberate off-by-default state pending sign-off, not a bug, but CSI should have visibility into when/whether it gets turned on.

# Maintenance, Configuration, and Troubleshooting {#sec-maintenance}

## Configuration Authority

::: {.callout-important}
**Correction to how this was originally scoped**: this document previously promised "one single
config file" for everything. That turned out not to match what was actually built. There are, in
practice, **two different kinds of settings, in different kinds of files, needing different levels
of comfort with computers to touch**:

| Kind of setting | Where it lives | Can a non-technical person safely edit it? |
|:---|:---|:---|
| The wording the AI is instructed to write reports with (tone, jargon rules, what counts as HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW) | Three plain-English `.txt` files — see table below | **Yes.** These are literally sentences of instructions, no code. Open in Notepad/TextEdit, edit the English, save. |
| Which AI model version is used, and the numeric thresholds that decide which competitors are even eligible to be scored | `pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/agent/orchestrator.py` (model version) and `pipelines/ci_model/shared/config.py` (thresholds) | **No.** These are Python program files. A misplaced comma or quotation mark breaks the whole tool with a technical error, not a friendly warning. Route any change here through a technical contact. |
| API keys and credentials (Anthropic, Google Maps) | Environment variable files (`.env.local`, not committed to the repository) | **Partially.** Setting up an account and generating a key is a one-time task best done by CSI's technical contact (see "Setting Up the Google Maps API Key" below), but no code is edited — it's account setup, not programming. |

There is no custom point-and-click settings screen for either category — see the update tools in
this chapter for the parts of the system that DO have a proper web screen (those are a completely
separate set of things: adding competitors, pits, and bid results, not these settings).
:::

## Configuration Parameters

| Common Change | File to Edit | Who Should Do It |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Change how the AI is told to write (tone, banned jargon, what counts as a "likely" bid) | `pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/prompts/system_prompt.txt` | Anyone — plain English text file |
| Change the wording of the per-competitor writeup instructions | `pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/prompts/polish_prompt.txt` | Anyone — plain English text file |
| Change what the AI's self-check step looks for | `pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/prompts/reflection_prompt.txt` | Anyone — plain English text file |
| Change which AI model version is used | `pipelines/ci_model/06_reporting/agent/orchestrator.py`, the line reading `_LLM_MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-6"` | Technical contact only — this is inside program code |
| Change which competitors are eligible to be scored at all (lookback windows, recency windows) | `pipelines/ci_model/shared/config.py`, the `V3_*` values near the top of the file | Technical contact only — tied to how the trained model itself was built; changing without understanding the model risks silently breaking predictions |
| Set up or rotate the Google Maps API key (pit-list map and geocoding) | `apps/web/.env.local`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` | Technical contact — requires a Google Cloud Console account and billing setup, see "Setting Up the Google Maps API Key" below |

## Handling New Competitors, Mergers, and Name Variants

**This one has a real web page — no code, no command line.** Go to the **Competitor names** page
(`/competitor-registry` in the web app). It works like a contact list with a merge function:

1. **New competitor appears in a bid.** Click **"Add competitor"** (top right), type the company's
   name into **"Canonical company name"** (optionally tag it if it's one of CSI's known top
   competitors), and save. If a very similar name already exists, the page will warn you before you
   add a duplicate — read that warning before clicking through it.
2. **Company merger, acquisition, or rebrand.** Select the old name(s), type the correct/surviving
   company name into the **"Target canonical name"** box, and click **"Consolidate"** — this merges
   their bid history under the one name going forward, it does not delete history.
3. **Wrong entry, typo, or a name that should never have been added.** Click the trash-can icon on
   that row. You'll be asked to confirm ("Confirm remove" / cancel) before anything is actually
   deleted — nothing is removed on the first click.

::: {.callout-important}
Skipping the confirmation prompts, or adding many names at once without reviewing each one, risks
one company's real bid history getting split across multiple different name entries. Every stat this
system produces for that company (bid rate, win rate, capacity) would then be based on only part of
their real history, and there would be no error message telling you this happened — it would just
quietly look like a smaller, less active company than it really is. Take the extra ten seconds on
each confirmation prompt.
:::

## Pit / PID Location Updates

Also a real web page: **Aggregate pit locations** (`/pit-list`). To add a pit: click **"Add pit"**,
enter its **Latitude**/**Longitude** (county and state fill in automatically once you enter
coordinates), pick who owns/has access to it, and save. There's also a **"Find nearest pits"** panel
if you want to check what's near a specific project or address before adding anything new. Editing
an existing pit uses the pencil icon on its row; deleting uses the trash-can icon, with the same
confirm-before-delete pattern as the competitor page above.

## Setting Up the Google Maps API Key

The pit-list page's interactive map and its coordinate-to-county/state auto-fill both call Google's
Maps JavaScript API and Geocoding API directly from the browser (@sec-solution-architecture) — this
is the one part of the system that is not proxied through CSI's own backend, so it needs its own key,
separate from the Anthropic API key the rest of the system uses. This is a one-time setup task for
CSI's technical contact:

1. Go to Google Cloud Console (`console.cloud.google.com`) and sign in with the account CSI wants to
   own this under — ideally a CSI company Google account, not a personal one, since billing and
   access live here long-term.
2. Create or select a project — the project dropdown in the top-left → **"New Project."** Name it
   something identifiable, e.g. "CSI Bid Intelligence."
3. Enable billing on that project (**Billing** in the left sidebar) — the APIs below won't activate
   without it. Google's free monthly credit comfortably covers this app's expected usage.
4. Enable the two required APIs — **"APIs & Services"** → **"Library,"** search for and enable both:
   - **Maps JavaScript API** (renders the interactive pit-list map)
   - **Geocoding API** (coordinate ↔ address lookups)
5. Create the key — **"APIs & Services"** → **"Credentials"** → **"Create Credentials"** →
   **"API key."** Google generates it immediately.
6. **Restrict the key.** This matters — it is a public, browser-exposed key, not a private secret:
   - Click into the new key → **Application restrictions** → **"HTTP referrers (web sites)"**
   - Add CSI's actual domain(s), e.g. `https://yourapp.com/*` — and `http://localhost:3000/*` if
     anyone will ever run the app locally
   - Under **API restrictions**, select **"Restrict key"** and check only the two APIs enabled in
     step 4
7. Set it in `apps/web/.env.local` as `NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY=<the key>`.

::: {.callout-important}
The referrer restriction in step 6 is what makes it safe for this to be a `NEXT_PUBLIC_*`
(browser-visible) key. Without it, anyone who views the page source could copy the key and run up
usage against CSI's own billing. Do not skip that step to "get it working faster."
:::

Also a real web page: **Bid results** (`/bid-results`). Two ways to use it:

- **Editing an already-recorded result**: click directly on the cell you want to change in the
  table — it edits in place, like a spreadsheet cell.
- **Entering results for a brand-new project** (one with no results recorded yet): the page shows a
  list of such projects on the left — search for it, click it, then for each company that bid, type
  the **"Bidder name"** and **"Bid amount"**. Click **"Add bidder"** to add more rows as needed. The
  page automatically shows a trophy icon on whichever row currently has the lowest bid amount (that's
  who it will record as the winner) — check that this matches what you actually know before saving.
  Click **"Save results"** when done.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Important — this does NOT currently feed into the report generator described in @sec-report-guide,
even though it may look and feel like it should.** Entries made on this page are saved live to CSI's
shared database, and DO immediately affect the numbers shown in the browser-based plan-upload chat
tool (if CSI uses that tool). But the separate, file-based report generator in @sec-report-guide
reads its own historical-data files, which are a **different copy** that is not automatically
refreshed from this page. A newly entered bid result will not show up in a report generated the way
@sec-report-guide describes until someone with technical access re-exports/regenerates those files.
Ask your technical contact how often that refresh happens, or request it explicitly before relying on
a just-entered result showing up in a generated report. **The competitor-names page above is the one
exception** — corrections made there DO have a working (if manual) pull-back process into the report
generator's data; bid results and pit locations do not have that yet.
:::

## When to Rerun the Pipeline

Re-run the report generator (@sec-report-guide) when:

- You need an updated report for a project and it's been a while since the last one was generated
  for it.
- Someone has confirmed (with your technical contact, per the warning above) that the underlying
  historical-data files have actually been refreshed with new bid results, pit locations, or
  competitor-name corrections — re-running before that refresh happens will just reproduce the same
  report with the same old data.
- A technical contact has changed one of the settings in @tbl-common-config-changes.

Updating the three web pages above (competitor names, pit locations, bid results) does **not**
itself require re-running anything — those changes save immediately when you click save/confirm.

## Troubleshooting Guide

| Symptom | Likely Cause | What To Do |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Red/orange error text ending in `FileNotFoundError` when running the report generator | One of the file-path lines in the command was typed differently than shown in @sec-report-guide (a changed quote mark, a missing dash) | Re-copy the exact command block from @sec-report-guide rather than retyping it by hand |
| Red/orange error text ending in `ValueError: No rows found for project_natural_key=...` | The project key doesn't match any row in `data/processed/projects.csv` | Re-open that file and re-copy the `project_natural_key` value exactly — do not type it from memory |
| Report generated with no written explanation sentences, just numbers | This is expected, not an error, when no AI service key is configured on the machine — the tool says so and falls back automatically | Nothing to fix unless CSI specifically wants the written narrative version; ask your technical contact to confirm the AI service key is set up |
| A newly entered bid result / pit / competitor correction isn't showing up in a generated report | The web pages and the report generator read different copies of the data (see the warning above) | Confirm with your technical contact whether/when the underlying files were refreshed |
| A competitor's stats look wrong (win rate, bid rate) | Their bid history may be split across two different name entries | Check the Competitor names page (`/competitor-registry`) for a near-duplicate name that should be merged |
| Pit-list page shows "Set `NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` in `apps/web/.env.local` to enable the map" instead of the map | The Google Maps API key has not been set up on this deployment | Follow "Setting Up the Google Maps API Key" above — a technical contact needs to do the one-time Google Cloud setup |
| Any error message not covered above | — | Do not guess/retry repeatedly — bring the exact error text to a technical contact |

: Troubleshooting guide. {#tbl-troubleshooting}

## Recommended Review Process

Before treating any generated report as ready to act on:

1. Confirm the project name/county/date at the top of the report matches the project you meant to
   check.
2. If any bid results or pit corrections were recently entered on the web pages, confirm with your
   technical contact that they were pulled into the report generator's data before this run — see
   the warning above.
3. Skim the Priority Competitors' deep dives against what your own team already knows — flag, don't
   silently accept, anything that looks off (@sec-output-files, Recommended Interpretation Rules).
4. If the report includes AI-written explanation sentences, spot-check at least one against the
   numbers directly above it in the same block, to confirm the sentence isn't claiming anything the
   numbers don't support.
5. Only after 1–4: use the report to inform a bid/no-bid discussion. Per @sec-limitations, this
   system is decision **support**, not a decision-maker — the final call is still CSI's.

# Limitations and Assumptions {#sec-limitations}

## This Is a Handoff, Not Ongoing Support

CSI will run this system on its own infrastructure and its own cloud API key after a 1–2 week transition window. There is no ongoing consulting relationship built into this deliverable. Any issue not covered by this document, the config file, or the troubleshooting guide will require CSI's own engineering/analytics resources to resolve, or a new, separately scoped engagement.

## Why Automated Bid-Result Email Parsing Was Scoped Out

Automated parsing of bid-result emails was considered and explicitly **not** built into this system. Bid-result notifications arrive in inconsistent formats across different letting authorities and vendors, with no reliable, universal structure to parse against — and critically, a silent mis-parse (a wrong bid amount, a misidentified winner) would corrupt the same historical data used to train and evaluate every other part of this system, with no obvious signal that it had happened. Manual bid-result input was chosen instead because a manual-entry gap is at least visible as a gap — a project simply shows up as "missing results" in the Bid Results page (@sec-maintenance) until someone enters it, rather than silently carrying a wrong number forward into every downstream statistic.

## The User-Input Path Is Not Reconciled With the Model-Output Path

CSI's manually entered top-3 competitors are enriched but never automatically compared against the ML model's or rule-based benchmarks' own predictions. If the two paths disagree, nothing in the current system surfaces that disagreement — it would need to be checked manually.

## Winner Hit Rate Has Not Been Validated Against CSI's Stated ~90% Expectation

Testing to date suggests the system's Winner Hit Rate, especially for any single rule-based factor evaluated without pre-filtering, falls well short of CSI's informally stated ~90% benchmark. This should be treated as an open, unresolved question rather than something this engagement definitively solved — the specific numbers behind this finding are internal experiment results not yet approved for external/client-facing use as final figures; see the data-integrity callouts in @sec-methodology and @sec-key-findings before citing a specific percentage.

## No Custom Configuration UI

All configuration changes require directly editing the config file. This was a deliberate scope decision to keep the system simple and auditable, not an oversight — but it does mean CSI needs someone comfortable editing a structured text/code file to make changes.

## No Independent Ground Truth for "Who CSI Considers a Real Competitor"

The rule-based and ML models are evaluated against who actually bid historically, not against CSI's own informal mental model of "real" competitors. The user-input path is the closest proxy for capturing that mental model, but it is not used as a training or evaluation label anywhere in the current system.

## The File-Based Report Generator Is Only Partially Bridged to Plan Reader

As described in @sec-solution-architecture, the live, in-browser report and the separate file-based CLI report generator (@sec-report-guide) are not equally connected to Plan Reader. The live report is scored directly from a plan's own just-verified data, pulled straight from the same shared database Plan Reader writes into. The file-based report generator is a different, older tool: it reads mostly-local files and a `--project-key` typed by hand, and only its Capacity bullet is pulled live from that shared database. It cannot today generate a standalone `.md`/`.docx` report for a project that exists only as a Plan-Reader-verified database row — that project would first need to reach the local files the CLI tool reads, the same "different copy, needs refresh" limitation already described for bid results and pit locations in @sec-maintenance.

## CI-Data Admin Features Are Not Yet Verified Against a Live Production Database

The three web update utilities (@sec-maintenance — competitor names, pit locations, bid results) and the underlying database connection they share were built and passed all automated code checks, but have not yet been run end-to-end against CSI's real production database in the environment they were developed in. CSI's own first real use of each utility after handoff should be treated as its first live verification, not as a known-working feature — flag anything that behaves unexpectedly to a technical contact rather than assuming it is user error.

## Some Extracted Bid-Item Quantities Are Withheld, Not Converted, by Design

Plan Reader can extract certain bid items measured in cubic yards or square yards (rather than the tons most of this system's material-quantity logic expects) but, as of this document's writing, does not automatically convert them into tons in a report — that conversion capability exists in the codebase but is deliberately switched off pending sign-off on the conversion formula and further validation. A report is explicit when this happens (it marks the affected quantity as withheld rather than silently showing zero), but it means a plan with, for example, a cubic-yard-measured base course may show a lower material total than the plan actually specifies. Estimators should treat "withheld" quantity notes as a prompt to check the source plan directly, not as "there is no such item."

## Plan Reader's Automated Coordinates Only Work for Six States

The automated latitude/longitude lookup (@sec-solution-architecture) only covers Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa, and Montana — the six states this system's DOT GIS integration was built against. A plan from any other state produces no automated coordinates at all; only a human-entered value fills that gap, through the same verification step used for every other field. This is a hardcoded geographic limit of the coordinate lookup specifically, distinct from the six-state dataset scope described in @sec-executive-summary — expanding either one is a separate piece of work.

## A Successful Verification Does Not Guarantee the Plan Reached the Shared Database

After an estimator confirms a plan's extraction, Plan Reader attempts to write that verified record into the shared `scratch.bid_projects` database (@sec-solution-architecture) — but that write is deliberately best-effort: if it fails (a network issue, a database hiccup), the verification step itself still reports success, and nothing in the current interface tells the estimator the underlying database write didn't happen. A plan could be fully verified in the browser and still not be durably recorded. This fail-open behavior was a deliberate choice — a database hiccup should never block an estimator from finishing their review — but it means an occasional silent gap between "verified in the UI" and "actually landed in the shared database" is possible, and there is no user-facing signal to catch it.

## The Live Web App's Candidate-Pool Logic Is a Hand-Maintained Copy, Not Shared Code

Because `apps/` and `pipelines/` intentionally do not import from each other (@sec-solution-architecture), the live web app's competitor-scoring code re-implements 6 of the CI team's candidate-eligibility signals by hand, separately from the actual `pipelines/ci_model` code that defines them. If a technical contact changes one of the `V3_*` values in @appendix-config-dictionary, or the CI team's own candidate-filtering logic changes, the live app's predictions can silently drift out of sync with what this document describes unless someone updates both places by hand. There is an automated test that catches this drift, but only when run against a live database connection — it is not something that fails loudly in day-to-day use.

## A Region With No Bid History Does Not Produce an Empty Result — It Falls Back to CSI's Nationwide Priority List

If a project falls in a state or region with no bid history on record, the candidate pool does not come back empty. It falls back to CSI's own ~25 flagged priority competitors, scored on their history from wherever they actually have bid — producing a normal-looking, fully-formed report for a location the system genuinely has no local competitive data on. Nothing in the report distinguishes this case from a well-supported prediction. An estimator reviewing a report for an unfamiliar or newly-covered region should specifically check whether the named competitors have any real presence there, rather than assuming the report's confidence reflects real local data.

## A State DOT Service Outage and a Genuinely Bad Route Number Look Identical Today

The state DOT GIS lookups behind Plan Reader's coordinate feature (@sec-solution-architecture) can return a technical error disguised as a normal empty response. When that happens, the system reports the same "route not found — check the route number and milepost" message it would give for an actual data-entry mistake in the plan. In practice this means a temporary outage at a state DOT's own mapping service can look, to an estimator, exactly like a plan that was extracted wrong — worth knowing before spending time re-checking a route number that was never the actual problem.

## The Competitor Registry's Priority Flags Are a Data-Dependent Safety Floor, Not a Guaranteed One

The ~25 companies flagged as CSI's own priority competitors in the registry are what keeps the candidate pool from ever coming back completely empty, even for a project with unusually sparse history. This floor exists because of the data currently in the registry, not because the code guarantees it — if those priority flags were ever cleared or lost through the Competitor Names update utility (@sec-maintenance), that protection would disappear with no alert telling anyone it happened. This is one more reason the confirmation prompts on that page (@sec-maintenance) matter beyond just avoiding duplicate names.

# Future Recommendations {#sec-future-recommendations}

## Short-Term Recommendations

- Confirm which capacity-rule variant (`capacity_volume` vs. the rejected `capacity_size_fit`) is the intended production default — see @sec-methodology, Methodology Notes and Validation Items.
- Run the CI-data admin web utilities (@sec-maintenance) against CSI's real production database as the first live verification pass — see @sec-limitations.
- Expand pit/PID location and ownership coverage beyond Minnesota, and beyond the current 10.8%-known-ownership rate within Minnesota, to materially improve the distance-based rule — see @sec-key-findings, Finding 2.

## Medium-Term Recommendations

- Revisit automated bid-result ingestion if a reliable, consistently-formatted data source is identified — the manual-entry decision (@sec-limitations) was a data-integrity choice, not a permanent one.
- Decide whether/when to enable the CY/SY quantity-conversion feature currently built but switched off pending sign-off (@sec-limitations).
- Build the pull-back path that lets manually entered pit locations and bid results (not just competitor-registry corrections) flow back into the file-based report generator's local data, closing the "different copy, needs refresh" gap described in @sec-maintenance.

## Long-Term Recommendations

- Build a reconciliation/comparison view between CSI's client-entered top-3 picks and the model's own predictions, so disagreement between "what I think" and "what the model thinks" (@sec-limitations) is surfaced automatically instead of requiring a manual check.
- Fully bridge the file-based report generator to Plan Reader (@sec-limitations), so a freshly uploaded, human-verified plan can generate a standalone `.md`/`.docx` report without first needing to exist in the CLI tool's local files.
- Explore whether a combined rule+ML ensemble, or an expanded feature set validated against a larger, multi-year dataset, closes more of the gap toward CSI's stated ~90% intuition (@sec-key-findings, Finding N).
